name: Signal flags for maritime communication
note: Flags of different colours and patterns, read at distance. First step beyond simple smoke: it is quick, daylight-reliable, and needs no line-of-sight relay network. A ship can read flags from another ship miles away. Codebook is implicit in sailor tradition.

name: Codebook for optical signal tower
note: Not the tower itself, but the agreed language it speaks. Without a standardised codebook (a government document), each tower operator invents his own alphabet. The innovation is making it systematic: three-position arms encode 8 letters per second in groups (like Morse). Requires coordination across the empire.

name: Optical semaphore tower
note: Tall wooden or brick tower with rotating wooden arms on three axes (shutter positions: open, half, closed). Operator turns cranks to set position, next tower sees it through telescope, relays instantly. No power needed. Can send 20 words per minute across 100 km chain. The killer innovation: a message travels the length of France in hours instead of weeks.

name: Heliograph - sun mirror telegraph
note: A polished mirror reflects sunlight to encode Morse dots and dashes. Works in daylight at range up to 50 km. Lighter and cheaper than optical towers. Cannot work at night or in cloud. The constraint is weather: an overcast day stops all communication, but the apparatus itself is simpler and more portable.

name: Morse code - dot, dash, space encoding
note: Morse code is not a hardware innovation; it is a language for the telegraph. Dots and dashes match the sounder's 'click' and 'hold', encoded by hand at the key. The genius is that it is rhythmic and acoustic: a skilled operator hears the message, not reading visual symbols. Fast hands can send 30 words per minute.

name: Morse register - recording apparatus
note: An electromagnetic solenoid pulls a stylus down onto a paper tape moving past it. When current flows, the dot or dash is recorded as a mark. The register was the original telegraph receiver: it married mechanical motion to electrical signal. A human operator then reads the tape and transcribes the message. The key limitation: without a sounder (sound output), it was slow to read and error-prone.

name: Morse sounder - audio telegraph receiver
note: A solenoid pulls an armature down onto a metal block (click), springs push it back (click). Morse is designed to be heard: a short current = dot sound, long current = dash sound. This was the killer innovation: skilled operators hear the message directly instead of squinting at paper tape. It increased speed tenfold. The sounder, not the relay, is the human interface to telegraphy.

name: Relay - current amplification for long lines
note: A weak current (from the distant telegraph key) flows through a solenoid, pulling a switch that closes a local circuit with a strong battery. This solves the fundamental problem: telegraph wire has resistance; after 100 km, the signal is too weak to operate the sounder. A relay at each station regenerates the signal at full strength. Without relays, the telegraph network stops at about 50 km. With relays, it can span continents.

name: Telegraph power supply - voltaic cells in series
note: Telegraph stations need reliable, large current (amps, not milliamps). A Daniell cell or Grove cell in series provides 1-2 volts. A telegraph key and relay need about 1 amp at 10-100 volts. The maintenance burden is high: cells need refilling, electrodes corrode, acid must be managed safely. This cost and complexity drives later adoption of central powerhouses.

name: Duplex telegraphy - simultaneous two-way transmission
note: A simple telegraph line is half-duplex: one side transmits while the other listens. Duplex uses a bridge circuit (Wheatstone bridge) to cancel your own transmitted signal at your receiver, so you hear only the far end. The trick: send your signal balanced (symmetrical) through two wires to ground so your receiver sees it as zero, but the asymmetrical current flowing through the line carries the signal. Doubles line capacity.

name: Quadruplex telegraphy - four signals on one wire
note: Quadruplex uses two independent duplex channels on the same wire: one at high current (positive), one at low current (negative). Requires precise impedance matching and filtering. The circuit is fragile (crosstalk is constant enemy), but it quadruples capacity. Thomas Edison's major telegraphy innovation. Marginal returns made it uneconomical by the 1900s, but it did prove the principle: multiplex the line, not the wire.

name: Submarine telegraph cable
note: A copper core (signal), wrapped in gutta percha (insulator), wrapped in steel armour, laid on the ocean floor. PROBLEM: Gutta percha is unobtainable (tropical tree). SUBSTITUTE: Use rubber-impregnated cloth (expensive) or pitch-soaked jute, accepting higher leakage. The cable capacitance is enormous; signals attenuate and blur over 3000 km. Needs a relay every 500 km, but submersion makes access impossible. Solution: repeater amplifiers at each end only.

name: Loading coil - range extension for telegraph lines
note: A coil of wire inserted periodically into a long telegraph or telephone line. Wire acts as a capacitor that stores charge; the coil inductance smooths it out. This compensates for cable distortion and allows signals to travel further before attenuation kills them. A loading coil every 2 km extends range from 50 km to 500 km on a submarine cable. The physics is: inductance and capacitance in series form a filter that attenuates high frequencies (noise) less than the signal distortion.

name: Carbon microphone - pressure-to-resistance transducer
note: Sound waves move a diaphragm that presses down on loose carbon granules. Pressure changes resistance. A steady current through the carbon, modulated by this resistance change, creates a modulated signal that can be sent down a telegraph wire. The key: carbon is cheap, robust, and changes resistance reliably from 100 to 1000 ohms with pressure. Early telephone transmitters were simple and effective.

name: Diaphragm receiver - electromagnet hearing aid
note: A thin iron diaphragm is magnetized by an electromagnet. Modulated current in the coil varies the magnetic field, moving the diaphragm in and out, creating sound waves. No power source needed at the receiver (signal current from the microphone drives it). Early telephone receivers were just magnets and thin iron discs, very similar to telegraph sounders. The diaphragm must be flat enough and thin enough to vibrate freely at audio frequencies.

name: Manual switchboard exchange
note: A grid of copper jacks (one per subscriber line), with plug cords and a central battery supplying current to all lines. An operator plugs a caller's line into the called party's line, completing a circuit. The breakthrough: no longer does each person need a separate wire to every other person. A central office with 100 operator positions can switch 10,000 customers with 100 lines. Manual exchanges require hundreds of staff and are limited by operator speed (one plug per second).

name: Trunk lines - long-distance telephone routes
note: Heavy-gauge copper wire strung on poles between cities, with loading coils every 2 km. A trunk line connects two exchanges, not individual subscribers. Calls are routed: local exchange A -> trunk to distant exchange B -> local delivery. The killer problem: telephone signals attenuate badly over distance. A 50 km trunk line needs repeater amplifiers every 15 km, which requires vacuum tubes (not available until 1915). Before that, trunk lines were limited to 50-100 km range.

name: Multiplexing - combining multiple signals on one line
note: Time-division multiplexing: 4 calls take turns using the same trunk line, each getting 1/4 of the time (switching at 1000 Hz, fast enough that voice sounds continuous). Frequency-division: use different frequency bands on the same line. Both require precision filters and were impractical until vacuum tube amplifiers. The principle: more calls per cable = more revenue per infrastructure dollar.

name: Strowger automatic exchange - mechanical switching
note: A caller dials pulses on the handset (1=one pulse, 2=two pulses, etc). These pulses drive a stepper motor which rotates a wiper across a grid of contacts, selecting the called party's line. No human operator needed. The 1890 Strowger exchange was a mechanical marvel: 100 stepper units could handle 10,000 lines. Reliability was marginal (mechanical wear, misalignment), but no wage bill. Replaced manual exchanges over 30 years. The real innovation is replacing human labor with electromechanics.

name: Stock ticker - financial telegraph terminal
note: A telegraph receiver modified to print stock prices and ticker symbols on a paper tape instead of requiring manual transcription. A ticker in each brokerage receives the same broadcast telegraph signal from the exchange, all printing simultaneously. The innovation is not technical but economic: it creates a new product (real-time pricing data) and a new business model (subscription service). The telegraph system becomes a data distribution network.

name: Spark transmitter - radio broadcast generator
note: A high-voltage battery (5000 V) charged a capacitor that discharged across an air gap, creating a spark. The spark radiates radio waves across a broad spectrum. A telegraph key interrupts the spark stream, encoding Morse code. Inefficient (most energy is heat and light), unreliable (spark gap is erratic), and creates tons of radio interference across all frequencies. But it works and requires no vacuum tubes. Replaced by continuous wave (CW) generation after 1915.

name: Crystal set receiver - galena rectifier radio
note: A tuned coil and capacitor select one radio station, a galena rectifier converts the RF signal to audio (crystal detects, headphones reproduce). No power source needed (rectified signal drives headphones directly). Range is short (5 km), quality is poor (strong local station only), but the cost is near zero. Crystal sets were toys in 1910, but mass-produced for every youth by 1920. They taught radio to the world, but they are obsolete once vacuum tube amplifiers exist.

name: Antenna and ground system for radio
note: An antenna is just a wire at a height or length that couples to the air (transmitting) or the air couples to it (receiving). A ground is a connection to earth (literally a copper plate or rod buried 2 metres). Radio waves need an antenna and a return path (ground) to form a closed loop. The antenna length determines efficiency at a given frequency. This was not obvious: early radio pioneers accidentally discovered that tall antennas worked better. Design theory came later.

name: Tuned LC circuit and resonance
note: An inductor (coil) and capacitor in series, tuned so that capacitive and inductive reactances cancel at a chosen frequency. At resonance, the impedance is minimum (current maximum), and the circuit selects only that frequency, rejecting others. This is THE solution to radio crowding: without tuning, all radio stations interfere. With tuning, each receiver selects one station and rejects the rest. Frequency = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). A variable capacitor lets listeners tune across the band.

name: Continuous wave (CW) generation with triode
note: A triode acts as an amplifier: a small signal on the grid amplifies a large signal in the anode. Fed back to the grid through a tuned circuit, this creates sustained oscillation (feedback), generating continuous RF at the resonant frequency. The generator is stable, efficient, and clean (no spark noise). Morse code is sent by turning the oscillator on/off with a telegraph key. Continuous wave replaced spark transmitters by 1920.

name: Triode oscillator - audio and RF frequency synthesis
note: A triode with feedback can generate any frequency from audio (10 Hz) to microwave (1000 MHz), tuned by the LC circuit. The oscillation amplitude is limited by the triode's power supply and efficiency. Used in radio transmitters, local oscillators for superheterodyne receivers, and audio oscillators for music synthesis. The triode is THE electronic oscillator until solid-state transistors arrive.

name: Amplitude modulation (AM) - encoding audio on radio
note: A microphone signal (audio, 0-10 kHz) is added to the RF oscillator output, varying its amplitude. The modulated wave is transmitted; a receiver detects the envelope (the modulation) using a rectifier, recovering audio. The trick: a 1 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio produces sidebands at 999 kHz and 1001 kHz. Radio stations are spaced 10 kHz apart (AM broadcast). The bandwidth is about 2x the audio frequency. Simple and robust.

name: Superheterodyne receiver - fixed intermediate frequency design
note: Instead of amplifying the RF signal directly (hard at high frequencies), a mixer combines the received signal with a local oscillator, producing a difference frequency (intermediate frequency, typically 455 kHz or 10.7 MHz). Tuning changes only the local oscillator; the intermediate frequency is fixed and easy to amplify. This is the most important radio innovation after AM: it made high-gain, selective receivers practical. Nearly all radio since 1920 is superheterodyne.

name: Frequency modulation (FM) - superior radio broadcast
note: Audio signal varies the frequency of the RF carrier instead of the amplitude. A 100 MHz carrier modulated with 1 kHz audio swings ±75 kHz. FM is immune to amplitude noise (static, ignition noise), so reception is much quieter. Bandwidth is about 10x wider than AM (200 kHz for 15 kHz audio), requiring wider channel spacing. Requires sophisticated receivers (discriminators, limiters). Adopted late (1940s in consumer radio) due to infrastructure cost, but ultimately superior.

name: Broadcasting as an institution - scheduled transmission and profit model
note: Not a technical innovation but an economic and political one. Broadcast stations transmit on fixed schedules so listeners know when to tune in. Content (music, news, drama) is produced by local staff. Revenue comes from advertising (selling commercial time). This is a radical model: entertainment and information are free to the listener, paid for by advertisers. By 1930, broadcasting is the dominant communication medium and has shaped politics, culture, and commerce.

name: Cathode ray tube (CRT) - electron beam display
note: An evacuated glass tube with a heated cathode that emits electrons, accelerated by 10,000 V towards a phosphor-coated anode. The electron beam is steered by magnetic coils (X and Y deflection). Where the beam hits the screen, the phosphor glows. Varying the beam current modulates the brightness. This is the display technology that made electronic television possible. The key: the beam is fast (MHz), allowing full-screen raster scanning at video rate.

name: Mechanical television scanning - early image transmission
note: A spinning disc with holes arranged in a spiral (Nipkow disc) scans an image line by line. Light from the scene passes through a hole onto a selenium photocell, which modulates current proportional to brightness. This signal is transmitted by radio; a receiver feeds it to a similar spinning disc, with light shining behind it, reconstructing the image on a screen. The whole system is mechanical, unreliable, and limited to about 30 lines of resolution. Electronic television replaced it by 1935.

name: Electronic camera tube (iconoscope) - real-time image capture
note: A vacuum tube where an electron beam scans a photosensitive mosaic (thousands of tiny silver-mica capacitors). Light on each capacitor charges it; the beam discharges each spot sequentially, producing a current proportional to light. This is a camera: it converts an optical image to an electrical signal suitable for transmission. The iconoscope was unreliable (mosaic damage, burn-in), but it launched electronic television and was the standard for decades.

name: Raster scan and synchronisation
note: The beam scans left-to-right (fast sweep), then retraces to the left (blanking), then drops one line down (slow sweep). It repeats 60 times per second (60 Hz frame rate), scanning 525 lines (NTSC) or 625 lines (PAL). At the receiver, an oscilloscope (CRT) must scan in exact synchronism. A sync pulse in the transmitted signal tells the receiver when each line begins and when each frame begins. Without tight synchronisation, the image tears and jitters. This is engineering at the microsecond level.

name: Magnetron - compact high-power microwave generator
note: A thermionic tube with a hot cathode that emits electrons, a strong axial magnetic field that curves them into a circular path, and resonant cavities around the periphery. Electrons oscillate between cavities, exchanging energy with the RF field. The result: very high power (kilowatts) at very high frequency (microwave, 9 GHz). Compact because the wavelength is tiny. Invented in 1939, it was classified as a weapon; it made radar practical for aircraft detection.

name: Waveguide - pipe for microwaves
note: At microwave frequencies (GHz), conventional wires radiate their signal into space (useless). A rectangular copper tube confines the microwave to propagate only in the TM01 mode (specific to the tube dimensions). Loss is low, and the signal is contained. Waveguide is like a plumbing system for microwaves: you assemble it with flanges and bolts, couple to a magnetron at one end and an antenna at the other. This solved the long-standing problem of transmitting high-frequency signals over distance.

name: Tetrode vacuum tube - screen grid amplifier
note: A triode with an added fourth electrode (screen grid), held at a positive but lower voltage than the anode. The screen shields the anode from the control grid, preventing feedback and allowing higher gain without oscillation. A tetrode is more stable and more powerful than a triode, better for RF amplifiers. The voltage between screen and cathode must be regulated, adding circuit complexity. By the 1930s, tetrodes replaced triodes in most high-power applications.

name: Pentode vacuum tube - suppressor grid output stage
note: A tetrode with a fifth electrode (suppressor grid, at cathode potential) that prevents secondary electrons from the anode reaching the screen. This was a problem in tetrodes (screen current wasted power). A pentode has higher efficiency and better linearity. It became the standard audio output tube and RF power tube from 1930 onward. Five or more grids became common in specialized tubes (hexode, heptode) for mixing and frequency conversion.

name: Coherer - primitive radio detector
note: A tube of glass filled with iron filings between two metal plugs. When RF current (from a radio signal) passes through, the filings cohere (stick together), dropping resistance from 1 megohm to 1000 ohms. A relay responds to this current change, signalling the received dot or dash. After each signal, a tapper mechanically shakes the tube to decohere the filings. Unreliable and slow (tapping delay), but it was the only radio detector before solid-state rectifiers.

name: Slide rule - mechanical multiplier
note: Two wooden rules with logarithmic scales, aligned by hand and compared visually. To multiply 5*7, you find 5 on one scale and 7 on the other, align them, and read 35 off the fixed scale. Uses the log identity: log(a*b)=log(a)+log(b). Accuracy is 3 digits, good enough for engineering work. Ubiquitous by 1900, slide rules were the dominant calculation tool until electronic calculators (1970s). Simple, cheap, and fast enough for design iteration.

name: Napier's bones - calculating rods
note: Rods with multiplication tables engraved in rows (one rod for each digit 0-9). To multiply 45*67, lay out the 4 and 5 rods, read the rows for 6 and 7, add diagonally. Reduces multiplication to table-lookup and addition. Slow compared to memorized multiplication, but eliminates error. Used by merchants and accountants. Fell out of use by 1700 as slide rules became popular, but conceptually important (separation of the multiplication table into components that can be recombined).

name: Stepped drum - mechanical counter and incrementor
note: A drum with 10 pins at different radial distances (0 to 9 steps). A rotating arm engages the appropriate pin and lifts a counter register once per turn. Used in Pascal's and Leibniz's calculators to perform addition and carry-over (successive addition is multiplication). The stepped drum was a brilliant mechanical innovation, but hand-cranked operation was tedious. Every mechanical calculator from 1600 onward used this principle or something similar.

name: Mechanical calculator - Pascal and Leibniz designs
note: A desktop mechanism with gears and stepped drums that performs addition, subtraction, and multiplication by repeated addition. Operator cranks and manipulates dials. Precision is critical: gears must mesh smoothly, and carries must propagate correctly through multiple decades. Hand-made calculators were expensive (200+ hours labor) and slow (1 operation per minute). But they were used by accountants for payroll and bookkeeping.

name: Arithmometer - mass-produced mechanical calculator
note: The first calculator to reach mass production (thousands made, not just hundreds). Uses standardized parts, precision jigs, and assembly-line methods. Reduced price from 500 denarii to 100 denarii. The Arithmometer (1851 onward) was the accountant's standard tool until electric calculators appeared (1960s). The innovation was not mechanical (same as Pascal's design) but manufacturing: making them cheaply and reliably.

name: Comptometer - key-driven calculator
note: Instead of a crank (one operation per second), the Comptometer (1887 onward) uses keys (one per digit). Pressing a key lever multiple times increments that digit, accumulating the sum. Touch typists could use Comptometers almost as fast as they thought of numbers. Faster than Arithmometer. The innovation is that the operator interface is ergonomic and intuitive (press 5 five times to add 5), not just mechanical optimization.

name: Difference engine - mechanical polynomial solver
note: A mechanism that uses the method of differences to evaluate polynomials and tabulate mathematical functions. Babbage built a working prototype in 1832, but the complete engine was never finished. Reason: tolerances. Brass expands and contracts with temperature (5 metres of machinery spans 0.5 mm over 10 degrees Celsius), cams wear, precision degrades. 19th century machine tools could hold 0.1 mm tolerances; the engine needed 0.01 mm consistency. It was engineering overreach, not a bad idea.

name: Analytical engine - programmable mechanical computer
note: Babbage's design for a universal mechanical computer: a large mill (arithmetic unit) and store (memory), programmed by punched cards like Jacquard looms. It could perform any sequence of arithmetic operations, conditional on intermediate results. The killer insight: a general-purpose machine can solve many problems if programmed differently. Ada Lovelace sketched an algorithm for it (1843). It was never built (same tolerance problems as the Difference Engine), but it was the conceptual foundation of the stored-program computer.

name: Jacquard loom - punched card control
note: A loom with thousands of vertical threads (warp). A deck of punched cards controls which threads are lifted on each pass of the shuttle. Complex patterns (brocade, damask) can be woven automatically. This was the first programmable machine: change the cards and the output changes. The innovation is separating control (the cards) from mechanism (the loom). This idea was revolutionary and inspired Babbage's Analytical Engine.

name: Hollerith tabulation - punched card data processing
note: Punched cards record data (census: age, occupation, birthplace, etc., each in a column). A machine reads the holes and closes electromagnetic switches, incrementing counters. The 1890 U.S. Census was tallied in months instead of years. This created data processing as an industry: IBM emerged from tabulating machines. The insight: data can be stored and processed mechanically, and this is faster than manual accounting.

name: Teleprinter - automated telegraph typing
note: Operator types on a keyboard (like a typewriter). Solenoids pull levers that position type wheels for each character, a hammer fires on command, the character prints on paper, and the whole sequence is transmitted as electrical pulses down the telegraph line. The receiving teleprinter receives the same pulses and reproduces each character. No skilled Morse operator needed; anyone who can type can use a teleprinter. Slower than Morse (40 words/minute vs. 100+), but usable by clerical staff.

name: Baudot code - 5-bit telegraph encoding
note: Each character is encoded as 5 binary digits (bits): mark (current) or space (no current). Letters, numbers, and symbols each have a 5-bit code. A teleprinter has 5 solenoids, one per bit. All 5 are energized simultaneously on reception, positioning the 5 levers correctly, and a mechanical stroke fires the type. This is the first digital telegraph code and the ancestor of modern binary encoding (ASCII, etc.). Standardized by the ITU in 1874.

name: Boolean algebra - logic and switching equivalence
note: Boolean algebra: true/false, AND, OR, NOT. Claude Shannon's insight (1938): switching circuits are Boolean algebras. A series switch is AND (both must be closed), parallel is OR. This is the single most important conceptual link in computing: abstract logic is isomorphic to physical electronics. Once realized, designing computers becomes designing logic circuits, which become routine engineering. No breakthrough in physics or chemistry needed, just the right mathematical language.

name: Binary arithmetic - base-2 number system
note: Binary: digits 0 and 1 only. Addition, multiplication, and logic are all simpler in binary than decimal. A two-state device (relay on/off, transistor on/off) represents 0 or 1 directly. Decimal requires devices with 10 states (complex and error-prone). All electronic computers use binary for this reason. The conceptual link: binary numbers are data, Boolean logic is control, they use the same substrates (switches).

name: Flip-flop circuit - one-bit memory
note: Two relays (or vacuum tube stages) cross-coupled: output of one feeds input of the other. The system has two stable states: relay A on and B off, or vice versa. A pulse on 'Set' line (via a contact closure) fires relay A, which holds itself on. A pulse on 'Reset' line fires relay B, which forces A off. This is a one-bit storage element: it 'remembers' whether it was last set or reset. The flip-flop is the foundation of all memory and state machines.

name: Register - multi-bit storage and transfer
note: Multiple flip-flops (one per bit) cascaded: an 8-bit register holds 8 bits. A control pulse transfers data into the register (latch), or shifts the data left/right (shift register). Registers are the basic building blocks of CPU architecture: accumulator (for arithmetic), memory buffer (for I/O), instruction register (for control). Every arithmetic operation reads from registers and writes back to them.

name: Ring counter - timing and sequencing circuit
note: A shift register with the output of the last stage fed back to the input. A single 1-bit propagates around the ring. On each clock pulse, the 1 moves to the next position. This generates a sequence of pulses on N different output lines, one line active at a time. Used for timing and sequencing in computers: generating control signals for memory access, ALU operations, etc. Simple and reliable, particularly in relay computers.

name: Accumulator - arithmetic work register
note: A register connected to an adder circuit (carries propagate left through carry-look-ahead or similar). A number can be added to the accumulator in one clock cycle. Repeated additions multiply (accumulate a number N times), division by repeated subtraction. The accumulator is the primary work register in early computers, used for nearly all arithmetic. Later CPUs generalize this to multiple general-purpose registers.

name: Relay computer - automated logic and arithmetic
note: A computer built entirely from relays (Zuse Z1-Z3, 1930s-1940s). Thousands of relays form registers, accumulators, and adders. A paper tape feeds instructions, step by step. The computer executes addition and subtraction in one second per operation. Multiply takes 20 seconds. The machine works, but it is slow, loud, and unreliable (relays stick, wear out). Replaced by vacuum tube computers (1000x faster) by 1950. The relay computer proved the principle: automation of calculation is feasible.

name: Vacuum tube computer - high-speed electronic switching
note: ENIAC (1945): 18,000 vacuum tubes, 150 kilowatts, does 5,000 additions per second (instead of 1 per second with relays). The tube acts as an electronic switch: no moving parts, microsecond speed. The killer limitation: reliability. Tubes fail constantly (one failure every 30 minutes). Maintenance requires replacing tubes and debugging. This drove the search for a smaller, more reliable switch: the transistor.

name: Magnetic wire storage - first practical memory
note: Steel wire wound on a reel, magnetized by a coil (1 bit = magnetized forward or backward). Access time is slow (wait for the right section of wire to pass the read/write head, like tape), but storage is cheap and non-volatile (data survives power loss). Used for audio recording and computer memory (1940s-1950s). Superseded by magnetic tape (cheaper) and later by core memory (faster). The innovation: ferromagnetism stores data, not mechanical position.

name: Magnetic tape storage - bulk archival memory
note: Paper or plastic tape coated with iron oxide, wound on reels. Data is stored sequentially (cannot directly access the middle). Cheap storage for large datasets (gigabytes on a compact reel). Speed is slow (minutes to locate a record). Used for daily backups, program storage, and archival data. IBM's System/360 (1965) relied on tape for I/O. Magnetic tape remained standard until optical media and solid-state storage arrived.

name: Magnetic core memory - fast addressable RAM
note: Toroidal ferrite cores (0.5 mm) arranged in a 2D grid (64x64 cores = 4096 bits). Each core stores 1 bit (magnetized clockwise or counter-clockwise). Access time is 1 microsecond (1000x faster than tape). Each core is addressed by X and Y wires (select row and column), read and write wires complete the circuit. Core memory was the standard for mainframe computers (1960s-1970s) until semiconductor RAM replaced it. Handwiring a core array took weeks.

name: Magnetic drum storage - early rotating memory
note: A cylinder coated with iron oxide, rotating at 3600 RPM. Read/write heads are stationary, positioned around the drum. Average access time is half a rotation (8 ms). Faster than tape, but requires synchronization with the rotating medium. Used as main memory in early computers (1950s) and later as auxiliary storage. Eventually replaced by moving-head disk drives (faster, fewer mechanical issues).

name: Semiconductor diode - p-n junction rectifier
note: A junction between p-type (hole-doped) and n-type (electron-doped) semiconductor. Forward bias allows current flow (low resistance), reverse bias blocks it (high resistance). Used as rectifier (AC to DC), detector, and digital switch. Silicon and germanium diodes were reliable by 1952. In logic, diodes replace vacuum tubes: smaller, cooler, longer-lived. The key is that the diode's threshold voltage sets the logic swing (0-5V typical).

name: Logic gate - elementary switching circuit
note: A circuit that implements Boolean logic: AND (output high if all inputs high), OR, NOT, NAND, NOR. Diodes and resistors suffice for simple gates. Transistors give active amplification (necessary for cascading gates). By the 1960s, logic gates were the design vocabulary for digital systems. A computer is built by combining gates into larger functions (adder, multiplier, controller). The innovation is recognizing that Boolean algebra and circuits are the same thing.

name: Photolithography - precision pattern transfer
note: UV light exposes a photoresist layer (thin polymer) through a mask. Exposed regions polymerize, unexposed regions dissolve. The pattern is then etched into the silicon with acid, creating trenches and ridges. This process repeats dozens of times (layers of metal, oxide, silicon). Feature size starts at 10 micrometers (1970), shrinks to 1 micrometer (1980), 0.1 micrometer (1995), and continues. Photolithography is the core of all semiconductor manufacturing.

name: Integrated circuit - many transistors on one chip
note: A single silicon chip (1 cm square) with thousands of transistors and resistors, interconnected by metal lines. The Small Scale Integration (SSI, 1960s) level put 10-100 components on a chip. Later: LSI (1000-10000), VLSI (millions), and beyond. The innovation is not a single transistor but the entire ecosystem: design tools, fabrication processes, testing, and assembly. One chip replaces a circuit board full of discrete components. Cost per transistor drops exponentially.

name: Stored program computer - code as data in memory
note: The conceptual breakthrough: a program is data. Instead of hand-rewiring circuits (ENIAC, 1945), the program sits in memory as numbers. The computer fetches each instruction, decodes it, and executes it. Changing the program is trivial (rewrite memory). This is Babbage's Analytical Engine concept finally realized in electronics. Every computer since has this architecture (von Neumann). This distinction (code vs. data, processor vs. memory) is fundamental.

name: Compiler and high-level programming language
note: A language like FORTRAN or ALGOL (not machine code) that expresses computations in human terms. A compiler translates source code to machine code. The breakthrough: programmers no longer need to think in bits and registers. They write mathematics and logic directly. Compilers handle optimization, memory allocation, and code generation. FORTRAN (1957) became the standard for scientific computing. This raised the abstraction level from machines to problems.

name: Error detecting and correcting codes
note: Parity bit (odd/even) detects single-bit errors. Hamming codes detect and correct single-bit errors. More powerful codes (Reed-Solomon, convolutional) can correct multiple errors. Used in memory (cosmic ray bit flips), transmission (noise corruption), and storage (magnetic media decay). The principle: add redundancy (extra bits) that encodes a checksum. On reception, recompute the checksum; if it mismatches, an error occurred and can be located/corrected.

name: Information theory - entropy and the bit
note: Shannon's theory (1948): information is measured in bits (binary digits). Entropy quantifies the average number of bits needed to encode a message. A channel's capacity (bits per second) sets the maximum transmission rate. Compression algorithms reduce redundancy (entropy coding). This theory unified communication, storage, and computation under one mathematical framework. Every modern system (networks, storage, codes) is designed using information theory.

name: Substitution and polyalphabetic ciphers
note: Caesar cipher (shift alphabet by N) was known to Rome. Vigenere cipher (shift depends on a repeating key) was stronger (1553 onward). Both are vulnerable to frequency analysis (common letters are obvious). The Vigenere cipher remained unbroken until the 19th century (Kasiski examination), making it militarily useful for 300 years. Encryption was the luxury of armies and empires; telegraph traffic required it, making cryptography a core technology.

name: Rotor cipher machine - Enigma and successors
note: A rotor (circular disk) with internal wiring that implements a substitution. As you type, each rotor rotates one position (like an odometer), changing the substitution. Three to five rotors in sequence give enormous key space (26^N combinations). The Enigma machine (1923 onward) was adopted by German military and was believed unbreakable until codebreakers (Turing, Rejewski) found flaws. The rotor machine was the standard for military encryption until electronics arrived.

name: One-time pad - information-theoretically secure cipher
note: A random key, used once, added to plaintext bit-by-bit (XOR). No amount of codebreaking can recover the plaintext without the key (Shannon's proof, 1945). The catch: you must generate, securely transmit, and store a key as long as the message. For millions of messages, this is impractical (key logistics). Used for highest-security traffic (Red Phone, diplomatic cables). The OTP is the gold standard, but its key distribution is a nightmare.

name: Public-key cryptography - RSA and successors
note: A key pair: public key (known to all) encrypts, private key (secret) decrypts. Asymmetric encryption (different keys for encode/decode) solves key distribution: no need to send a shared secret. RSA (1977) bases security on integer factorization (hard for large numbers). Each party publishes their public key; anyone can encrypt for them, only they can decrypt. This invented secure communication without pre-shared keys: revolutionary for email, web, and digital signatures.
